rationale: Both call finding a good wife a fortunate gift: Sirach pronounces her husband happy, while Proverbs says he has found favors and gladness from God.
source_text: Happy is the husband of a good wife, and the number of his days is doubled.

target_units.text: One who found a good wife found favors, and received gladness from God.

rationale: Sirach's courageous wife gives her husband a peaceful life; Proverbs describes the courageous woman as trustworthy to her husband and doing him good throughout life.
source_text: A courageous wife gladdens her husband, and he will complete his years in peace.

target_units.text: A courageous woman—who will find her? Such a woman is more precious than costly stones.
Her husband’s heart is confident in her; such a woman will not lack fine spoils.
For she works good things for her husband throughout her life.

rationale: Sirach places a good wife among the Lord's gifts to those who fear Him; Proverbs distinguishes inherited property from the wife whom God joins to a husband.
source_text: A good wife is a good portion; she will be given among the portion of those who fear the Lord.

target_units.text: Fathers apportion house and property to children, but a wife is joined to a husband by God.

rationale: The good heart and cheerful face in Sirach correspond to Proverbs' rejoicing heart and flourishing face; the outward expression follows the inward condition in both.
source_text: Whether rich or poor, his heart is good, and at every time his face is cheerful.

target_units.text: When the heart rejoices, the face flourishes, but when it is in sorrows, the face grows gloomy.

rationale: Sirach fears collective hostility and false accusation; the council's search for false testimony against Jesus supplies a particular instance of assembled accusers pursuing a deadly charge.
source_text: My heart feared three things, and before a fourth presence I made supplication: a city’s slander, an assembled mob, and a false accusation—all more grievous than death.

target_units.text: The chief priests and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus to put Him to death,
but found none, although many false witnesses came forward. Finally two came forward

rationale: Sirach connects jealousy between wives with household anguish. Rachel's envy of her sister and distressed demand for children illustrate that rivalry, without identifying her with every detail of Sirach's warning.
source_text: A wife jealous of another wife is heartache and mourning, and a scourge of the tongue that reaches everyone.

target_units.text: And Rachel saw that she had borne no children to Jacob, and Rachel envied her sister, and said to Jacob, “Give me children, or I shall die.”

rationale: Both sayings portray a harmful spouse through dangerous animals: grasping a scorpion in chapter 26 corresponds to chapter 25's preference for living with a lion and dragon over an evil woman.
source_text: An evil wife is a shifting ox-yoke; the one who takes hold of her is like someone grasping a scorpion.

target_units.text: I would choose to live with a lion and a dragon rather than live with an evil woman.

rationale: Sirach warns that drunkenness exposes a wife's shame; Proverbs describes drinkers' bruises, crooked speech, exposure, and loss of awareness. The warning about intoxication is shared, though Proverbs addresses drinkers more broadly.
source_text: A drunken wife is great wrath, and she will not conceal her shame.

target_units.text: Who has woe? Who has uproar? Who has a lawsuit? Who has unpleasantness and chatter? Who has bruises for nothing? Whose eyes are livid?
Is it not those who linger over wines? Is it not those who track down where drinking parties take place?
Do not become drunk with wine, but associate with righteous people, and converse during walks; for if you give your eyes to bowls and cups, afterward you will walk about barer than a pestle.
But at the end he lies stretched out as though struck by a snake, and as though by a horned viper its poison spreads through him.
When your eyes see another woman, then your mouth will speak crooked things,
and you will lie down as in the heart of the sea, and like a helmsman in heavy surging;
and you will say, “They strike me, and I felt no pain; they mocked me, but I did not know. When will dawn come, so that I may go and seek those with whom I will gather?”

rationale: Sirach associates the woman's eyelids with sexual misconduct; Proverbs warns against being seized by a woman's eyelids in its surrounding warning about sexual temptation. Both make the gaze part of that warning.
source_text: A woman’s sexual immorality will be known in the lifting of her eyes and in her eyelids.

target_units.text: Do not let desire for beauty overcome you; do not be hunted by your own eyes, nor seized by her eyelids.

rationale: Both passages expressly require a firm watch over a headstrong daughter. Chapter 42 expands the warning by describing the household's public shame, while chapter 26 emphasizes her use of freedom.
source_text: Keep a firm watch over a headstrong daughter, so that she does not find freedom and use it for herself.

target_units.text: Keep a firm watch over a headstrong daughter, lest she make you a delight to enemies, a subject of talk in the city, and an outcast of the people, and put you to shame among a great multitude.

rationale: Sirach warns the hearer to be on guard in connection with a shameless eye and possible offense. Proverbs warns against desire and being captured by a woman’s eyelids; in their surrounding sexual warnings, both make the gaze a matter for vigilance.
source_text: Be on guard after a shameless eye, and do not marvel if she offends against you.

target_units.text: Do not let desire for beauty overcome you; do not be hunted by your own eyes, nor seized by her eyelids.

rationale: Sirach depicts sexual indiscrimination as drinking from every nearby water; Proverbs commands drinking from one's own vessels and keeping the waters exclusive. The water imagery serves opposite patterns of sexual conduct.
source_text: Like a thirsty traveler she will open her mouth and drink from every nearby water; she will sit before every tent peg and open her quiver before an arrow.

target_units.text: Drink waters from your vessels and from your spring wells.
Do not let waters overflow for you from your spring; but let your waters travel into your own squares.
Let them belong to you alone, and let no outsider share with you.

rationale: Sirach describes a wife's grace and knowledge strengthening her husband. Proverbs likewise honors a courageous wife as his crown, then contrasts the destructive effect of a woman who does evil.
source_text: A wife’s grace will delight her husband, and her knowledge will fatten his bones.

target_units.text: A courageous woman is a crown to her husband; but as a worm in wood, so a woman who does evil destroys a man.

rationale: Sirach values a silent, disciplined wife as the Lord's gift; Peter values the wife's gentle and quiet inner spirit as precious before God. Both place worth on inward restraint.
source_text: A silent wife is a gift of the Lord, and there is no exchange for a disciplined soul.

target_units.text: but the hidden person of the heart, in the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious before God.

rationale: Sirach says no weight can match a modest, self-controlled wife; Peter contrasts external gold and clothing with the precious, imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet heart.
source_text: A modest wife is grace upon grace, and no weight is worth a self-controlled soul.

target_units.text: Let your adornment not be the outward kind—braiding hair, putting on gold ornaments, or dressing in garments—
but the hidden person of the heart, in the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious before God.

rationale: Sirach compares a good wife's beauty to the rising sun; the Song compares the beloved to dawn, moon, and sun. Both praise feminine beauty through heavenly light.
source_text: The sun rising in the Lord’s heights—so is a good wife’s beauty in the order of her house.

target_units.text: Who is this looking out like dawn, beautiful like the moon, chosen like the sun, a terror like troops drawn up?

rationale: The shining holy lampstand supplies Sirach's comparison for a beautiful face. Exodus describes the sanctuary lampstand and its lamps shining; the connection is the sacred object used as an image, not an identification of the woman with it.
source_text: A lamp shining upon a holy lampstand—so is a beautiful face upon a firmly established stature.

target_units.text: You shall make a lampstand of pure gold, of worked metal. Its stem, branches, bowls, knobs, and lilies shall be made from it.
Six branches shall extend from its sides, three from one side of the lampstand and three from the other.
There shall be three bowls shaped like little nuts, with a knob and lily on one branch. So it shall be for the six branches extending from the lampstand.
On the lampstand there shall be four bowls shaped like little nuts; on one branch shall be its knobs and lilies.
There shall be a knob under the two branches extending from it, and a knob under the four branches extending from it; so it shall be for the six branches extending from the lampstand.
Its knobs and branches shall be made from it, the whole worked from one piece of pure gold.
You shall make its seven lamps and set them on it, and they shall shine from one face.

rationale: Both describe bodily beauty through pillars resting on precious bases. Sirach uses gold pillars and a silver base for beautiful feet; the Song uses marble pillars and golden bases for the beloved's legs.
source_text: Golden pillars upon a silver base—so are beautiful feet upon the breast of one who stands firm.

target_units.text: his legs are marble pillars founded upon golden bases; his appearance is like Lebanon, choice as cedars,

rationale: One of Sirach's grievous sights is a righteous person turning to sin and facing judgment. Ezekiel likewise says that a righteous person's later injustice brings death despite earlier righteous acts.
source_text: At two things my heart has grieved, and at the third anger came upon me: a warrior in want through need, understanding men when they are treated as refuse, and someone turning back from righteousness to sin. The Lord will prepare him for the sword.

target_units.text: But when a righteous person turns from his righteousness and practices injustice according to all the lawlessness the lawless person committed, none of the righteous acts he did will be remembered. In the transgression he committed and the sins he sinned, in these he will die.

rationale: Sirach warns that trade readily becomes entangled with wrongdoing. Hosea joins an unjust balance, the claim to have become rich, and sinful labors, giving a particular example of corrupt gain.
source_text: A merchant will hardly be delivered from wrongdoing, and a retailer will not be acquitted of sin.

target_units.text: Canaan—in his hand is a balance of injustice; he loved to dominate.
Ephraim said, ‘Indeed I have become rich; I have found refreshment for myself.’ All his labors will not be found for him because of the injustices in which he sinned.

rationale: Sirach says the pursuit of profit leads many into sin; Paul describes the desire for riches as a snare and the love of money as leading people away from faith into many pains.
source_text: Many have sinned for profit, and the one who seeks to increase his gains will turn his eye away.

target_units.text: But those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all evils, and some, reaching for it, wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains.

rationale: Sirach locates sin between buying and selling; Hosea's unjust balance and sinful accumulation of wealth give concrete commercial form to that warning.
source_text: A peg will be fixed between the joints of stones, and sin will be squeezed between selling and buying.

target_units.text: Canaan—in his hand is a balance of injustice; he loved to dominate.
Ephraim said, ‘Indeed I have become rich; I have found refreshment for myself.’ All his labors will not be found for him because of the injustices in which he sinned.

rationale: Sirach warns that a house falls when its owner fails to hold fast to the Lord's fear; Proverbs contrasts disappearing impious houses with the standing tents of those who act rightly.
source_text: Unless a person holds fast diligently in the fear of the Lord, his house will quickly be overthrown.

target_units.text: The houses of the impious will disappear, but the tents of those who act rightly will stand.

rationale: Sirach's sieve image exposes a person's refuse through reasoning; Jesus says speech comes from the heart's abundance and makes the speaker accountable. Both treat expressed words as evidence of inner character.
source_text: When a sieve is shaken, refuse remains; so a person’s rubbish remains in his reasoning.

target_units.text: Brood of vipers! How can you speak good things when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.
The good person brings forth good things from the good treasure, and the evil person brings forth evil things from the evil treasure.
But I tell you that people will give account on the day of judgment for every idle word they speak.
For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

rationale: Sirach compares testing a person's deliberation with firing pottery; Proverbs compares the Lord's examination of hearts with testing precious metal in a furnace. Both use heat-testing to illuminate personal assessment.
source_text: A furnace tests a potter’s vessels, and a person’s testing is in his deliberation.

target_units.text: As silver and gold are tested in a furnace, so hearts are chosen before the Lord.

rationale: Both join a tree known by its fruit with speech revealing the heart. Sirach's cultivation and spoken thought correspond to Jesus' fruit, inner treasure, and mouth speaking from the heart's abundance.
source_text: A tree’s fruit reveals its cultivation; so a word reveals the thought of a person’s heart.

target_units.text: For no good tree produces rotten fruit, nor again does a rotten tree produce good fruit.
Each tree is known by its own fruit. People do not gather figs from thorns, nor harvest grapes from a bramble.
The good person brings out good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings out evil from the evil treasure; for his mouth speaks from the heart’s abundance.

rationale: Sirach postpones praise until a person has spoken and been tested; Proverbs condemns answering before hearing. Both require listening before forming an outward response rather than making a premature assessment.
source_text: Do not praise a man before he reasons, for this is the testing of human beings.

target_units.text: One who answers a word before hearing it—it is foolishness and reproach for him.

rationale: Sirach pictures attained righteousness as a glorious robe; Job says he clothed himself in righteousness and wrapped himself in justice like a double cloak. Moral conduct is worn as clothing in both.
source_text: If you pursue what is right, you will attain it and put it on like a glorious robe reaching to the feet.

target_units.text: I had clothed myself with righteousness, and I wrapped myself in justice like a double cloak.

rationale: Sirach 27's birds lodging with their own kind repeat the association principle stated in chapter 13: every living creature loves its like. The zoological comparison supports the surrounding discussion of human company.
source_text: Birds will lodge with their like, and truth will return to those who practice it.

target_units.text: Every living creature loves its like, and every person his neighbor.

rationale: Sirach depicts sin waiting like a lion for unjust people; Peter depicts the devil as a lion seeking someone to devour. The shared image is predatory danger requiring vigilance, with different agents named.
source_text: A lion lies in wait for prey; so sin lies in wait for those who do unjust things.

target_units.text: Be sober; be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.

rationale: Sirach characterizes godly discourse as wisdom; Proverbs says the righteous person's mouth drips wisdom. Both link the moral character of the speaker with wise speech.
source_text: A godly person’s discourse is always wisdom, but a fool changes like the moon.

target_units.text: The mouth of the righteous drips wisdom, but the tongue of the unjust will be destroyed.

rationale: Sirach recommends limiting time among the uncomprehending and lingering with thoughtful people; Proverbs contrasts walking with the wise and walking with fools. Both make chosen company consequential for wisdom.
source_text: Among people without understanding, watch the time; among thoughtful people, linger.

target_units.text: One who walks with the wise will be wise, but one who walks with fools will be known.

rationale: Sirach rejects fools' offensive discourse and indulgent laughter; Ecclesiastes likens fools' laughter to noisy thorns beneath a pot and calls it futile. Both strip foolish laughter of its apparent value.
source_text: Fools’ discourse is offensive, and their laughter is in sinful indulgence.

target_units.text: for like the sound of thorns beneath a cauldron, so is the laughter of fools. This too is futility.

rationale: Sirach depicts frequent oath-taking as disturbing speech associated with quarrels. Jesus directs hearers away from oaths toward plain yes and no, supplying a stronger restraint on the same speech practice.
source_text: The talk of someone who swears many oaths will make hair stand up, and their quarrel makes one stop the ears.

target_units.text: But I tell you: do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God,
nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of His feet, nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.
Nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.
But let your word be ‘Yes, yes’; ‘No, no.’ Whatever is beyond these is of evil.

rationale: Sirach connects proud quarrels with bloodshed and mutual abuse; Proverbs says a wrathful man digs up strife and an angry man digs out sins. Both connect quarrelsome behavior with further wrongdoing or harm.
source_text: The quarrel of the proud is bloodshed, and their mutual abuse is grievous to hear.

target_units.text: A wrathful man digs up strife, and an angry man dug out sins.

rationale: Sirach says exposing secrets destroys trust and close friendship; Proverbs contrasts a double-tongued revealer of plans with the faithful person who conceals matters. Confidentiality marks trustworthiness in both.
source_text: The one who reveals secrets has destroyed trust and will certainly not find a friend close to his soul.

target_units.text: A double-tongued man reveals plans in a council, but one faithful in breath conceals matters.

rationale: Sirach's command to keep faith with a friend is immediately threatened by revealing secrets; Proverbs identifies faithful conduct with concealing matters rather than disclosing them.
source_text: Love a friend and keep faith with him; but if you reveal his secrets, do not pursue him afterward.

target_units.text: A double-tongued man reveals plans in a council, but one faithful in breath conceals matters.

rationale: Sirach compares lost friendship with bereavement. David's grief for Jonathan gives a concrete expression of mourning a beloved friend; David's loss is through death, while Sirach uses that grief as an analogy for broken trust.
source_text: For as a person has lost his dead, so you have lost your neighbor’s friendship.

target_units.text: I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan. You were very beautiful to me; your love for me was wonderful, beyond the love of women.

rationale: Sirach pictures the lost friend as a bird released beyond recovery; Proverbs pictures escape from a guarantor's entanglement as a bird escaping a trap. Both use the freed bird, with different human situations in view.
source_text: As you have released a bird from your hand, so you have let your neighbor go, and you will not catch him.

target_units.text: so that you may save yourself like a gazelle from snares and like a bird from a trap.

rationale: The friend who has escaped like a gazelle from a trap repeats the escape image Proverbs uses for someone freeing himself from surety. Sirach stresses the pursuer's inability to recover the friend.
source_text: Do not pursue him, because he has gone far away and escaped like a gazelle from a trap.

target_units.text: so that you may save yourself like a gazelle from snares and like a bird from a trap.

rationale: Both distinguish repairable injury to friendship from disclosure of secrets. Chapter 22 allows return after a drawn sword but names secret-revealing among causes of flight; chapter 27 contrasts healing wounds with lost hope after betrayal.
source_text: For a wound can be bound up, and there is reconciliation after abuse, but the one who revealed secrets has lost hope.

target_units.text: If you draw a sword against a friend, do not despair, for there is a way back.

If you open your mouth against a friend, do not be afraid, for there is reconciliation—except for reproach, pride, disclosure of a secret, and a treacherous blow; at these things every friend will flee.

rationale: Both connect winking or signaling with the eye to a crooked person's schemes. Proverbs expands the gestures into a portrait of a lawless man continually devising evil.
source_text: The one who winks with his eye devises evil things, and no one will remove them from him.

target_units.text: A foolish and lawless man travels ways that are not good;
the same man signals with his eye and gives signs with his foot, and instructs by gestures of his fingers;
with a twisted heart he devises evils at every time. Such a person stirs up disturbances for a city.

rationale: Sirach's flatterer speaks sweetly in person but twists words afterward; Proverbs' enemy agrees with his lips while concealing deceit and hostility in his heart. Both expose agreeable speech masking harm.
source_text: Before your eyes he will make his mouth sweet and marvel at your words, but afterward he will twist his mouth and put a stumbling block in your words.

target_units.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;
if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.
One who hides enmity establishes deceit, but one well known in councils discloses his own sins.

rationale: In context Sirach names the deceptive flatterer as hated by the Lord. Proverbs includes the unjust tongue, evil schemes, false witness, and manufactured disputes among what the Lord hates.
source_text: I have hated many things, but compared none to him; the Lord will hate him too.

target_units.text: because he rejoices in everything the Lord hates, and is crushed because of his soul’s uncleanness:
an insolent person’s eye, an unjust tongue, hands shedding a righteous person’s blood,
and a heart devising evil thoughts, and feet hastening to do harm;
an unjust witness kindles falsehoods and sends disputes among brothers.

rationale: Sirach's stone thrown upward returns on the thrower's head; Proverbs' rolled stone returns on the roller. Both portray intended harm recoiling upon its initiator through a returning stone.
source_text: The one who throws a stone upward throws it upon his own head, and a treacherous blow will open wounds.

target_units.text: One who digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it, and one who rolls a stone rolls it upon himself.

rationale: Both expressly say that the person who digs a pit will fall into it. Sirach adds a setter caught in his own trap, extending the pattern of the action's adverse result returning on the actor. Ecclesiastes' surrounding examples also concern work hazards, so malicious intention is not assigned to its pit digger.
source_text: The one who digs a pit will fall into it, and the one who sets a trap will be caught in it.

target_units.text: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever tears down a fence will be bitten by a snake.

rationale: Both say that the person who digs a pit falls into the very hole he made. The psalm places this reversal within its account of injustice returning upon its maker.
source_text: The one who digs a pit will fall into it, and the one who sets a trap will be caught in it.

target_units.text: He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the hole he made.

rationale: Sirach says evil rolls back on its maker unexpectedly; Proverbs depicts the digger falling into his own pit and the rolled stone returning on its roller. The concrete images exemplify returning harm.
source_text: The one who does evil things will have them roll back upon him, and he will certainly not know where they have come to him from.

target_units.text: One who digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it, and one who rolls a stone rolls it upon himself.

rationale: Sirach says evil deeds roll back upon their maker; the psalm describes conceived injustice and trouble returning upon the offender’s own head. Both portray wrongdoing becoming the wrongdoer’s harm.
source_text: The one who does evil things will have them roll back upon him, and he will certainly not know where they have come to him from.

target_units.text: Behold, he was in labor with injustice; he conceived trouble and gave birth to lawlessness.
He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the hole he made.
His trouble will return upon his head, and his injustice will descend upon his crown.

rationale: Sirach places mockery, reproach, and pursuing retribution before the proud; Proverbs says insolence leads toward ruin. Both connect pride with the downfall that follows it.
source_text: Mockery and reproach await the proud, and retribution will lie in wait for him like a lion.

target_units.text: Insolence leads before ruin, and evil-mindedness before a fall.

rationale: Sirach warns that rejoicing at the godly person's fall ends in punishment. Obadiah forbids rejoicing over Judah's destruction and announces recompense returning on the offender's own head.
source_text: Those who rejoice at the fall of the godly will be caught in a trap, and pain will consume them before their death.

target_units.text: Do not look on your brother’s day, on the day of strangers; do not rejoice over the sons of Judah on the day of their destruction; do not speak boastfully on the day of affliction.

Do not enter the gates of peoples on the day of their suffering. You, too, must not look on their assembly on the day of their destruction, and do not join in attacking their strength on the day of their destruction.
Do not stand at their escape routes to destroy those of them who are being saved, and do not shut in those fleeing from them on the day of affliction.
For the day of the Lord is near against all the nations. Just as you acted, so it will be for you; your recompense will be repaid upon your own head.

rationale: Sirach calls resentment and wrath abominations held by a sinner; Ephesians commands bitterness, rage, anger, and malice to be removed. Both reject the deliberate retention of these dispositions.
source_text: Resentment and wrath—these too are abominations, and a sinful man will hold them fast.

target_units.text: Let all bitterness and rage and anger and shouting and slander be taken away from you, with all malice.

rationale: Sirach warns the avenger that the Lord will avenge and retain his sins; Romans prohibits self-avenging because repayment belongs to the Lord. Both place vengeance under divine judgment.
source_text: The one who takes revenge will find revenge from the Lord, and He will certainly keep his sins in view.

target_units.text: Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but make room for wrath; for it is written, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.”

rationale: Both explicitly connect forgiving others' wrongs with receiving divine forgiveness. Sirach places the connection in prayer, while Matthew states both the forgiving and unforgiving outcomes.
source_text: Forgive your neighbor’s wrong, and then when you pray, your sins will be released.

target_units.text: For if you forgive people their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.
But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

rationale: Sirach challenges asking the Lord for healing while keeping anger against another. The parable challenges a servant who receives mercy but refuses mercy to his fellow servant; both expose the inconsistency, though the parable speaks of debt rather than healing.
source_text: Does a person keep wrath against another person and seek healing from the Lord?

target_units.text: Then his master summoned him and said, ‘Evil slave! I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me.
Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I had mercy on you?’
His master became angry and handed him over to the torturers until he repaid everything owed.
So also My heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts.”

rationale: Sirach asks how someone without mercy for a fellow human can seek forgiveness for himself. The master in Matthew condemns precisely the servant who received mercy yet withheld it from his fellow servant.
source_text: Does he have no mercy on a person like himself and pray concerning his own sins?

target_units.text: Then his master summoned him and said, ‘Evil slave! I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me.
Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I had mercy on you?’
His master became angry and handed him over to the torturers until he repaid everything owed.
So also My heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts.”

rationale: Sirach questions atonement for a mortal who retains resentment; Matthew says the Father will not forgive the person who refuses to forgive others. Both confront persistent unforgiveness as an obstacle to receiving forgiveness.
source_text: If he himself, being flesh, keeps resentment, who will atone for his sins?

target_units.text: But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

rationale: Sirach joins remembrance of decay and death with keeping commandments. Ecclesiastes describes dust returning to earth and concludes with fearing God, keeping commandments, and awaiting judgment.
source_text: Remember the last things and stop being hostile; remember decay and death, and remain in the commandments.

target_units.text: and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
Futility of futilities, said Ecclesiastes; everything is futility.
Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.
Ecclesiastes sought much to find words of delight and something written in uprightness, words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads and like planted nails, which were given from collections, from one shepherd, and something beyond them.
My son, beware of making many books; there is no limit, and much study is weariness of the flesh.
The conclusion of the matter—the whole is heard: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole human being.
For God will bring every deed into judgment, concerning everything overlooked, whether good or evil.

rationale: Sirach's command not to resent a neighbor recalls the law's prohibition of vengeance and lasting anger against one's people, joined to loving the neighbor as oneself.
source_text: Remember the commandments and do not be resentful toward your neighbor; remember the covenant of the Most High and overlook ignorance.

target_units.text: And your hand shall not take vengeance, neither shall you remain angry with the sons of your people; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself; I am the Lord.

rationale: Sirach says avoiding quarrels lessens sins because temper kindles conflict; Proverbs links a wrathful man with strife and an angry man with sins. The same temper-to-conflict-to-sin sequence is present.
source_text: Keep away from quarrelling, and you will lessen sins, for a hot-tempered person will kindle a quarrel.

target_units.text: A wrathful man digs up strife, and an angry man dug out sins.

rationale: Sirach's sinner disrupts friends by slander; Proverbs' crooked man spreads evil and deceit and separates friends. Both identify malicious communication as a destroyer of relationships.
source_text: A sinful man will disturb friends and cast slander among those at peace.

target_units.text: A crooked man sends out evils, lights a torch of deceit for evil people, and separates friends.

rationale: Both compare the supply of fuel to the growth of a quarrel. Proverbs makes wood and coals correspond to the abusive person who sustains conflict; Sirach similarly connects increasing fuel and increasing strife.
source_text: As the fuel for a fire is, so it will burn; as a quarrel grows firm, so it will burn. A person’s anger will match his strength, and he will raise his wrath according to his wealth.

target_units.text: With much wood a fire flourishes, but where there is no double-minded person, battle is quiet.
A hearth for coals and wood for fire, and an abusive man for the turmoil of battle.

rationale: Sirach describes a hurried dispute as kindling fire and spilling blood; Proverbs makes an abusive person fuel for the turmoil of battle. Both give conflict the destructive action of a fed fire.
source_text: A hurried dispute kindles fire, and a rushing quarrel pours out blood.

target_units.text: A hearth for coals and wood for fire, and an abusive man for the turmoil of battle.

rationale: Sirach contrasts blowing a spark into fire with quenching it, both from the mouth. Proverbs likewise contrasts a yielding answer that turns wrath away with a painful word that stirs it up.
source_text: If you blow on a spark, it will burn; if you spit on it, it will be quenched. Both come out of your mouth.

target_units.text: Anger destroys even intelligent people; but a yielding answer turns away wrath, and a painful word stirs up anger.

rationale: Sirach condemns whispering and double speech for destroying peace; Proverbs describes a crooked speaker separating friends. Both trace communal damage to deceptive speech.
source_text: Curse a whisperer and someone double-tongued, for he has destroyed many who were at peace.

target_units.text: A crooked man sends out evils, lights a torch of deceit for evil people, and separates friends.

rationale: Sirach describes a destructive tongue scattering peoples and overturning houses; James describes the small tongue setting a great forest and the course of life ablaze. Both emphasize damage far larger than the speaking organ.
source_text: A third tongue has shaken many and scattered them from nation to nation; it has pulled down fortified cities and overthrown dignitaries’ houses.

target_units.text: So also the tongue is a small member and boasts great things. Look how small a fire sets so great a forest ablaze!
And the tongue is a fire. The tongue is established among our members as a world of unrighteousness, staining the whole body, setting the wheel of life ablaze, and itself set ablaze by Gehenna.

rationale: Sirach denies rest and quiet to someone who attends to destructive speech. Proverbs says conflict becomes quiet when the double-minded person is absent, showing the peace gained by removing its verbal fuel.
source_text: The one who attends to it will certainly not find rest or dwell in quiet.

target_units.text: With much wood a fire flourishes, but where there is no double-minded person, battle is quiet.

rationale: Sirach compares the tongue's injury with a lash and shattered bones; Proverbs says some people wound with a sword as they speak. Both describe verbal harm as bodily injury.
source_text: A lash’s blow makes a bruise, but a tongue’s blow will shatter bones.

target_units.text: There are those who wound with a sword as they speak, but the tongues of the wise heal.

rationale: Sirach attributes more deaths to the tongue than to the sword; Proverbs places death and life in the tongue's hand. Both assign speech power over life and death without making identical numerical claims.
source_text: Many have fallen by the edge of a sword, yet not as many as those who have fallen through a tongue.

target_units.text: Death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and those who control it will eat its fruits.

rationale: Sirach blesses the person sheltered from the destructive tongue; the psalm says God shelters His people in a tent from the contradiction of tongues. Both make safety from hostile speech a form of shelter.
source_text: Happy is the one sheltered from it, who has not passed through its anger, who has not pulled its yoke or been bound in its bonds.

target_units.text: Thou wilt hide them in the hiding place of Thy presence from human turmoil; Thou wilt shelter them in a tent from the contradiction of tongues.

rationale: The harmful tongue imposes iron and bronze bondage, whereas wisdom's fetters and collar become rest, shelter, and glory in chapter 6. The repeated restraint imagery distinguishes oppressive speech from beneficial instruction.
source_text: For its yoke is an iron yoke, and its bonds are bronze bonds.

target_units.text: Put your feet into her fetters and your neck into her collar.
Place your shoulder beneath her and carry her, and do not resent her bonds.
Approach her with all your soul, and keep her ways with your whole strength.
Trace her out and seek her, and she will become known to you; when you have gained hold of her, do not let her go.
For in the end you will find her rest, and she will turn to gladness for you.
Her fetters will become a strong shelter for you, and her collars a robe of glory.

rationale: Sirach says the destructive tongue will not master the godly; the psalm describes divine shelter from human turmoil and hostile tongues. Both place the protected person beyond the tongue's destructive rule.
source_text: It will certainly not master the godly, and they will not be burned in its flame.

target_units.text: Thou wilt hide them in the hiding place of Thy presence from human turmoil; Thou wilt shelter them in a tent from the contradiction of tongues.

rationale: Sirach portrays those abandoning the Lord as prey of destructive speech, likened to a ravaging animal. The psalm joins a warning about a talkative man with evils hunting the unjust person to destruction.
source_text: Those who abandon the Lord will fall into it; among them it will burn and certainly not be quenched. It will be sent against them like a lion and ravage them like a leopard.

target_units.text: A talkative man will not be set straight on the earth; evils will hunt an unjust man to destruction.

rationale: Sirach 28's instruction to secure property and precious metal corresponds to chapter 42's instruction to lock things where many hands are present. In chapter 28 this practical guarding prepares the following comparison with guarded speech.
source_text: Behold, fence your property with thorns; bind up your silver and gold.

target_units.text: With an evil woman, a seal is good; where there are many hands, lock things up.

rationale: Both expressly picture controlling speech as placing a door around the mouth: Sirach commands a door and bar, while the psalm asks the Lord for a guard and restraining door around the lips.
source_text: Make a balance and a weight for your words, and make a door and a bar for your mouth.

target_units.text: Set a guard, Lord, for my mouth and a restraining door around my lips.

rationale: Sirach warns that an unguarded mouth can cause a fall before an ambusher; Proverbs says guarding mouth and tongue keeps one's life from affliction. Both connect speech restraint with personal safety.
source_text: Take care lest you slip through it, lest you fall before someone lying in ambush.

target_units.text: One who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his life from affliction.

rationale: Sirach identifies lending to a neighbor with mercy and commandment-keeping; the psalm likewise calls compassionate lending the conduct of a kind man.
source_text: The one who shows mercy will lend to his neighbor, and the one who strengthens his hand keeps commandments.

target_units.text: Kind is the man who has compassion and lends; he will manage his words with judgment.

rationale: Sirach joins timely lending with timely repayment; the psalm contrasts the sinner who borrows without repaying with the righteous person's compassionate giving. Both distinguish honest help from exploitative borrowing.
source_text: Lend to your neighbor at his time of need, and in turn repay your neighbor at the appointed time.

target_units.text: The sinner borrows and will not repay, but the righteous person has compassion and gives.

rationale: Sirach tells the borrower to confirm his word and keep faith so help remains available. The psalm honors the person who does not set aside an oath to his neighbor, alongside integrity in financial dealings.
source_text: Confirm your word and keep faith with him, and at every time you will find what you need.

target_units.text: One who acts wickedly is held in contempt before him, but he honors those who fear the Lord; one who swears to his neighbor and does not set it aside.
He did not lend his silver at interest and did not take gifts against innocent people. The one who does these things will never be shaken.

rationale: Sirach describes borrowers who treat loans as windfalls and harm their helpers; the psalm identifies borrowing without repayment as sinful. Both address taking the benefit of a loan while refusing its obligation.
source_text: Many regarded a loan as a windfall and brought trouble upon those who helped them.

target_units.text: The sinner borrows and will not repay, but the righteous person has compassion and gives.

rationale: Sirach details a borrower's change from pleading to delaying payment and making excuses. The psalm's sinner who borrows but does not repay states the ethical failure embodied in that conduct.
source_text: Until he receives it, he will kiss the lender’s hands and lower his voice over his neighbor’s money; when repayment is due, he will drag out the time, return words of indifference, and blame the season.

target_units.text: The sinner borrows and will not repay, but the righteous person has compassion and gives.

rationale: The borrower in Sirach repays assistance with insults and dishonor; the psalmist receives slander, evil, and hatred in exchange for love and good. Both expose hostility returned for a benefactor's help.
source_text: If the lender succeeds, he will scarcely recover half and regard it as a windfall. If not, the borrower has deprived him of his money and made him an enemy for nothing. He will repay him with curses and insults, and repay dishonor in place of honor.

target_units.text: Instead of loving me, they were slandering me, but I was praying.
They set evils against me in exchange for good things and hatred in exchange for my love.

rationale: Sirach observes that fear of losing money deters lending, before urging continued help in the following verses. Jesus similarly challenges lending governed only by expected repayment and commands lending without expecting anything back.
source_text: Many have turned away, not from wickedness, but because they feared being deprived for nothing.

target_units.text: If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners to receive the equivalent back.
But love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing back. Your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, because He is kind to the ungrateful and evil.

rationale: Sirach says not to leave the lowly waiting for alms; Proverbs says not to send the needy away until tomorrow when one already has the means to help. Both reject avoidable delay in assistance.
source_text: Nevertheless, be patient with the lowly person and do not keep him waiting for alms.

target_units.text: Do not refrain from doing good to someone in need whenever your hand has the means to help.
Do not say, ‘Go away and come back; tomorrow I will give,’ when you are able to do good, for you do not know what the coming day will bring forth.

rationale: Sirach grounds support for the poor in the commandment and forbids sending them away empty. Deuteronomy commands openhanded lending to the needy brother and forbids withholding help out of self-interest.
source_text: For the commandment’s sake, support the poor person; in his need do not turn him away empty.

target_units.text: And if there is among you one of your brethren in need, within any of your cities in the land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not withhold the affection of your heart, neither shall you close your hand against your needy brother.
You shall freely open your hands unto him, and shall surely lend him as much as he needs, according to his want.

Take heed unto yourself, lest there be a hidden, lawless thought in your heart, saying: The seventh year, the year of release, draws near; and your eye be evil toward your needy brother, and you give him nothing, and he cry against you unto the Lord, and there be great sin upon you.

You shall freely give unto him, and shall surely lend him as much as he needs; and your heart shall not be grieved when you give unto him. For because of this the Lord your God shall bless you in all your works, and in all that you put your hand unto.

rationale: Sirach prefers spending silver for a brother or friend to letting it corrode unused. Jesus links giving alms with a lasting treasure beyond the reach of moth and theft, redirecting possessions toward help rather than hoarding.
source_text: Lose silver for a brother and a friend, and do not let it corrode under a stone to destruction.

target_units.text: Sell your possessions and give alms. Make for yourselves purses that do not wear out, an unfailing treasure in the heavens, where no thief draws near and no moth destroys.

rationale: Sirach locates worthwhile treasure in obedience to the Most High rather than gold's mere possession; Jesus contrasts vulnerable earthly treasures with treasure in heaven and links treasure to the heart's allegiance.
source_text: Place your treasure according to the Most High’s commandments, and it will benefit you more than gold.

target_units.text: Do not store up treasures for yourselves upon earth, where moth and consumption destroy and where thieves break through and steal.
But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor consumption destroys and where thieves neither break through nor steal.
For where your treasure is, there your heart will also be.

rationale: Sirach describes stored almsgiving as rescue in affliction. The psalm blesses care for the poor and needy and promises the Lord's rescue in an evil day, making generosity and protection correspond.
source_text: Store up almsgiving in your chambers, and it will rescue you from every affliction.

target_units.text: Blessed is the one who understands the poor and needy; in an evil day the Lord will rescue him.
May the Lord guard him, keep him alive and bless him in the land; may He not hand him over into his enemy’s hands.

rationale: In Sirach, almsgiving provides protection stronger than weapons against an enemy. The psalm joins care for the poor with the Lord's guarding and a plea not to be handed into the enemy's hands.
source_text: More than a strong shield and more than a weighty spear, it will fight for you against an enemy.

target_units.text: Blessed is the one who understands the poor and needy; in an evil day the Lord will rescue him.
May the Lord guard him, keep him alive and bless him in the land; may He not hand him over into his enemy’s hands.

rationale: Sirach commends the good man who stands surety for his neighbor. Judah's surety for Benjamin becomes an offer to remain enslaved in his place, a concrete instance of accepting another's liability.
source_text: A good man will stand surety for his neighbor, but someone who has lost shame will abandon him.

target_units.text: “For your servant became surety for the lad to his father, saying, ‘If I do not bring him to you and set him before you, I shall bear the guilt before my father all my days.’
“Now therefore I will remain with you as a servant in the lad’s place, a household slave to my lord; but let the lad go up with his brothers.
“For how shall I go up to my father if the lad is not with us? Let me not see the evils which shall befall my father.”

rationale: Sirach commends standing surety for another; Paul offers to have any debt Onesimus may owe charged to himself and personally promises repayment. The letter supplies an explicit offer of financial guarantee.
source_text: A good man will stand surety for his neighbor, but someone who has lost shame will abandon him.

target_units.text: And if he has wronged you in anything, or owes you anything, charge that to my account.
I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me even your own self.

rationale: Sirach stresses the guarantor's personal exposure on another's behalf. Judah, having guaranteed Benjamin to his father, offers himself as a household slave in Benjamin's place, showing what that responsibility can cost.
source_text: Do not forget a guarantor’s favors, for he has given his life on your behalf.

target_units.text: “For your servant became surety for the lad to his father, saying, ‘If I do not bring him to you and set him before you, I shall bear the guilt before my father all my days.’
“Now therefore I will remain with you as a servant in the lad’s place, a household slave to my lord; but let the lad go up with his brothers.
“For how shall I go up to my father if the lad is not with us? Let me not see the evils which shall befall my father.”

rationale: Sirach condemns the ungrateful person who ruins and abandons his guarantor; Proverbs condemns returning evil for good and attaches continuing harm to that reversal of kindness.
source_text: A sinner will overthrow a guarantor’s good circumstances, and someone ungrateful in thought will abandon his rescuer.

target_units.text: One who repays evil things instead of good things—evils will not move from his house.

rationale: Sirach warns that surety destroys formerly prosperous people. Proverbs warns against becoming a pledge without means to pay because even one's bedding may be taken, giving concrete form to financial collapse.
source_text: Surety has destroyed many who were prospering and shaken them like a wave of the sea.

target_units.text: Do not give yourself as a pledge out of deference to a face.
For if you have no means from which to pay, they will take the bedding from beneath your sides.

rationale: Sirach describes surety driving powerful people from home; Proverbs pictures a pledge costing the debtor his bedding. Both make the danger reach the guarantor's domestic security, though only Sirach describes exile.
source_text: It has driven powerful men from home, and they wandered among foreign nations.

target_units.text: Do not give yourself as a pledge out of deference to a face.
For if you have no means from which to pay, they will take the bedding from beneath your sides.

rationale: Sirach warns of a sinner entering surety and ending in lawsuits. Proverbs describes the guarantor as trapped by his own words and delivered through his friend into hostile hands, requiring urgent release.
source_text: A sinner who falls into surety and pursues profitable undertakings will fall into lawsuits.

target_units.text: Son, if you act as guarantor for your friend, you will give your hand over to an enemy.
For a man’s own lips are a strong trap, and he is caught by the lips of his own mouth.
Son, do what I command you and save yourself—for through your friend you have come into evil men’s hands. Go without growing slack, and press the friend for whom you acted as guarantor.

rationale: Sirach limits support to one's ability and warns against falling oneself. Paul accepts generosity according to what one has and rejects relief for others purchased by affliction for the giver.
source_text: Support your neighbor according to your ability, and take care of yourself so that you do not fall.

target_units.text: For if the readiness is present, it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have.
For it is not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you, but on the basis of equality:

rationale: Sirach lists bread, water, clothing, and shelter as life's first necessities. Paul likewise treats food and coverings as sufficient grounds for contentment, concentrating on basic provision rather than wealth.
source_text: The first necessities of life are water, bread, clothing, and a house that covers nakedness.

target_units.text: But having food and coverings, with these we will be content.

rationale: Sirach prefers a poor person's own shelter to splendid meals in others' homes; Proverbs prefers a peaceful morsel to a well-provisioned house with conflict. Both place a modest, secure condition above troubled abundance.
source_text: Better a poor person’s life beneath a shelter of beams than splendid dishes in other people’s homes.

target_units.text: Better a morsel with pleasure in peace than a house full of many good things and unjust sacrifices with battle.

rationale: Sirach commands contentment with little or much; Paul describes learning contentment both in abundance and need, whether filled or hungry. The contrasting material conditions are explicit in both.
source_text: Be content with little or much, and you will certainly not hear the reproach of living as a guest.

target_units.text: Not that I speak because of need, for I have learned to be content whatever my circumstances.
I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to be in need.

rationale: Sirach's dependent guest is displaced when a more honored guest arrives. Jesus describes the shame of surrendering one's place to a more honored invitee; the situations differ between lodging and seating but share humiliating displacement.
source_text: Go out, guest, before a more honored person; my brother has come as my guest, and I need the house.”

target_units.text: “When someone invites you to a wedding feast, do not recline in the foremost place. Someone more honored than you may have been invited by him,
and the one who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give this man your place.’ Then you will begin, with shame, to occupy the last place.

But when you are invited, go and recline in the last place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he will say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have honor before all who recline at table with you.

rationale: Both ancient sayings connect love for a son with parental discipline. Proverbs contrasts this with sparing the staff; Sirach adds the father's hoped-for joy in later days.
source_text: The one who loves his son will continually give him lashes, so that he may rejoice at his last days.

target_units.text: One who spares the staff hates his son, but one who loves him disciplines carefully.

rationale: Sirach says a disciplined son benefits his father and gives him grounds for public pride; Proverbs promises the disciplining parent rest and adornment to his life. Both portray a favorable parental result.
source_text: The one who disciplines his son will benefit from him and boast about him among acquaintances.

target_units.text: Discipline your son, and he will give you rest and give adornment to your life.

rationale: Sirach's father rejoices before friends over his taught son; Proverbs calls father and mother to rejoice over a wise son. The shared connection is parental joy arising from the child's formation.
source_text: The one who teaches his son will make his enemy envious and rejoice over him before friends.

target_units.text: A righteous father brings up well, and his life rejoices over a wise son;
let father and mother rejoice over you, and let the one who bore you be glad.

rationale: Sirach 30 pictures the dead father continuing through the son who resembles him. Chapter 44 describes descendants preserving the ancestors' inheritance and covenants while the buried ancestors' name lives through generations.
source_text: His father died, yet it is as though he did not die, for he left someone like himself after him.

target_units.text: It will remain with their offspring; their descendants are a good inheritance.
Their offspring stood within the covenants, and their children did so because of them.
Their offspring will remain for ever, and their glory will not be blotted out.
Their bodies were buried in peace, and their name lives through generations.

rationale: Sirach emphasizes a father's joy in seeing his son during life; Proverbs describes the righteous father's rejoicing over a wise son. Sirach extends that consolation to the father's death, which Proverbs does not separately address.
source_text: During his life he saw him and rejoiced, and at his death he was not grieved.

target_units.text: A righteous father brings up well, and his life rejoices over a wise son;
let father and mother rejoice over you, and let the one who bore you be glad.

rationale: Sirach's son inherits responsibility to answer enemies and repay friends' kindness. David's instructions to Solomon combine judgment on Joab and Shimei with mercy toward Barzillai's sons, illustrating both sides of that succession.
source_text: He left an avenger against enemies and one who would repay kindness to friends.

target_units.text: You also know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me, what he did to the two commanders of Israel’s forces, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He killed them, setting the blood of war in peace, and put innocent blood on the belt around his waist and the sandal on his foot.
Act according to your wisdom, and do not bring his gray hair down to Hades in peace.
Show mercy to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for they came near to me in this way when I fled from your brother Absalom.

Behold, with you is Shimei son of Gera, a son of the Benjaminite from Bahurim. He cursed me with a painful curse on the day I went to Camps. He came down to meet me at the Jordan, and I swore to him by the Lord, ‘I will not put you to death with the sword.’
You must certainly not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You will know what to do to him, and you shall bring his gray hair down to Hades with blood.”

rationale: Sirach warns that indulgence in raising a son brings distress to the parent's inward life. Proverbs contrasts corrective formation with a wandering child who shames his parents; both describe parental suffering from an unrestrained child.
source_text: The one who pampers a son will bind up his wounds, and at every cry his inward parts will be troubled.

target_units.text: Blows and reproofs give wisdom, but a wandering child shames his parents.

rationale: Sirach compares the unrestrained son's stubbornness with an untamed horse. Proverbs contrasts blows and reproof that teach wisdom with the wandering child who brings shame, likewise opposing formation to unchecked behavior.
source_text: An untamed horse turns out stubborn, and an unrestrained son turns out headstrong.

target_units.text: Blows and reproofs give wisdom, but a wandering child shames his parents.

rationale: Sirach says pampering a child brings the parent fear and grief; Proverbs says the wandering child shames his parents. Both warnings focus on the household consequences of failing to restrain the child.
source_text: Pamper a child, and he will terrify you; play with him, and he will grieve you.

target_units.text: Blows and reproofs give wisdom, but a wandering child shames his parents.

rationale: Sirach warns that indulgent familiarity can end in shared suffering and grief. Proverbs offers the opposite outcome through discipline: rest and adornment for the parent. The connection concerns the contrasting results of upbringing.
source_text: Do not laugh together with him, so that you do not suffer together and in the end gnash your teeth.

target_units.text: Discipline your son, and he will give you rest and give adornment to your life.

rationale: Sirach withholds authority from a son in youth. Paul's illustration likewise places the child heir under guardians and stewards until the father's appointed time, despite the child's status as master of everything.
source_text: Do not give him authority in youth.

target_units.text: Now I say that as long as the heir is a child, he differs in no way from a slave, though he is master of everything.
Rather, he is under guardians and stewards until the date appointed by his father.

rationale: Both texts present corporal discipline of a young child as preventative correction. Sirach names hardening and disobedience as the danger; Proverbs presents the rod as rescuing the child's life from death.
source_text: Bruise his sides while he is little, lest he become hardened and disobey you.

target_units.text: Do not refrain from disciplining a little child, for if you strike him with a rod, he will certainly not die;
for you will strike him with a rod, but rescue his life from death.

rationale: Sirach directs the parent to discipline the son to avoid suffering through his shamelessness. Proverbs commands discipline and describes the resulting rest and adornment of the parent's life.
source_text: Discipline your son and work upon him, so that you do not stumble through his shamelessness.

target_units.text: Discipline your son, and he will give you rest and give adornment to your life.

rationale: Sirach links bodily well-being with joy of heart as surpassing goods. Proverbs says a rejoicing heart makes a person flourish while sorrow dries the bones, directly connecting inward joy and bodily condition.
source_text: There is no wealth better than bodily health, and no gladness beyond joy of heart.

target_units.text: A rejoicing heart makes one flourish, but a sorrowful man’s bones dry up.

rationale: Sirach presents death as preferable to bitter life and enduring illness. Job asks why suffering people receive life when they long for death and rejoice to obtain it, expressing the same comparison from within anguish.
source_text: Death is better than a bitter life, and eternal rest than persistent illness.

target_units.text: For why has light been given to those in bitterness, and life to souls in pain,
who long for death and do not obtain it, digging for it as for treasures,
and become overjoyed if they obtain it?

rationale: Sirach's good food before a closed mouth depicts possessions that cannot be enjoyed. Ecclesiastes describes a rich owner whom God does not empower to eat from his own goods, exposing the same gap between having and enjoying.
source_text: Good things poured out before a closed mouth are like offerings of food set beside a tomb.

target_units.text: a person to whom God will give wealth, possessions and glory, so that his soul lacks nothing it desires, yet God will not empower him to eat from it, for a stranger will eat it. This is futility and a grievous sickness.

rationale: Sirach's comparison depends on an idol's inability to eat or smell. The psalm describes manufactured idols whose mouths do not speak and whose noses do not smell, supplying the same image of lifeless sensory incapacity.
source_text: What benefit is an offering to an idol? For it neither eats nor smells; so is the one pursued by the Lord.

target_units.text: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, works of human hands.
They have a mouth and will not speak; they have eyes and will not see.
They have ears and will not hear; they have noses and will not smell.

rationale: Sirach warns against handing the soul over to grief and tormenting oneself in thought. Paul directs anxiety into prayer and describes God's peace guarding hearts and thoughts, addressing the same vulnerable inner life with a distinct response.
source_text: Do not give your soul over to grief, and do not afflict yourself with your deliberation.

target_units.text: Be anxious about nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

rationale: Sirach says gladness of heart supports life and length of days; Proverbs says a rejoicing heart makes one flourish and contrasts sorrow's effect upon the bones. Both connect joy with vitality.
source_text: Gladness of heart is a person’s life, and a man’s rejoicing is length of days.

target_units.text: A rejoicing heart makes one flourish, but a sorrowful man’s bones dry up.

rationale: Sirach warns that grief destroys many and offers no benefit in the grief it describes. Paul also names sorrow that produces death, while expressly distinguishing beneficial godly sorrow leading to repentance; that distinction prevents equating all sorrow with harm.
source_text: Beguile your soul, comfort your heart, and put grief far from you; for grief has destroyed many, and there is no benefit in it.

target_units.text: For godly sorrow produces repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but the sorrow of the world produces death.

rationale: Sirach 30 says anger, jealousy, and anxiety shorten life and age a person. Chapter 38 likewise says grief brings death and bends strength, linking destructive inward distress with bodily decline.
source_text: Jealousy and anger shorten days, and anxiety brings old age before its time.

target_units.text: For death comes from grief, and grief of heart will bend strength.

rationale: Sirach connects a bright, good heart with taking care over food; Ecclesiastes directs eating bread with gladness and drinking wine with a good heart. Both connect a good heart with the manner of eating.
source_text: A bright and good heart will take care over the dishes it eats.

target_units.text: Come, eat your bread with gladness and drink your wine with a good heart, for God has already favored your deeds.

rationale: Both directly connect wealth with lost sleep: Sirach describes anxious wakefulness wasting the flesh, while Ecclesiastes says being filled with riches does not let the owner sleep.
source_text: Wakefulness over wealth wastes the flesh, and anxiety about it drives away sleep.

target_units.text: Sweet is the slave’s sleep, whether he eats little or much; but being filled with riches does not let him sleep.

rationale: Sirach continues the description of anxiety driving away sleep after its warning about wealth. Ecclesiastes likewise opposes restful sleep to the sleeplessness of being filled with riches; Sirach additionally mentions illness.
source_text: The anxiety of wakefulness will drive away drowsiness, and a severe illness will rouse a person from sleep.

target_units.text: Sweet is the slave’s sleep, whether he eats little or much; but being filled with riches does not let him sleep.

rationale: Sirach describes the rich person's labor accumulating money followed by luxurious rest. The rich man in Jesus' parable plans larger storehouses and then tells his soul to rest, eat, drink, and rejoice; the surrounding parable challenges that security.
source_text: A rich person toiled in gathering money, and at rest he is filled with his luxuries.

target_units.text: And he said, ‘This is what I will do: I will pull down my storehouses and build larger ones, and gather all the grain and my goods there.
And I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Rest, eat, drink, be glad!”’

rationale: Sirach says love of gold and pursuit of profits lead a person astray; Paul says desire for riches entraps people and love of money leads some away from faith into many pains.
source_text: The one who loves gold will not be justified, and the one who pursues profits will go astray in them.

target_units.text: But those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all evils, and some, reaching for it, wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains.

rationale: Sirach describes people ruined through gold; Paul says the desire for wealth plunges people into ruin and destruction. Both identify the pursuit of riches as a cause of personal collapse.
source_text: Many were given over to ruin for gold, and their destruction happened before their face.

target_units.text: But those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all evils, and some, reaching for it, wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains.

rationale: Sirach calls gold a stumbling block that catches the infatuated fool; Paul calls the desire for riches a snare accompanied by foolish and harmful desires. Both portray acquisitiveness as entrapment.
source_text: It is a stumbling block for those infatuated with it, and every fool will be caught by it.

target_units.text: But those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all evils, and some, reaching for it, wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains.

rationale: Sirach blesses the rich person who remains blameless without pursuing gold. Job rejects appointing gold as his strength or trusting riches, treating that misplaced confidence as grave lawlessness before God.
source_text: Happy is the rich person who was found blameless and did not go after gold.

target_units.text: If I appointed gold as my strength, or trusted in a costly stone,
if I rejoiced because much wealth came to me, or laid my hand upon countless things,
do I not see the shining sun fail, and the moon diminish? For it does not depend on them.
And if my heart was secretly deceived, or I placed my hand upon my mouth and kissed it,
may this also be reckoned to me as the greatest lawlessness, for I lied before the Lord Most High.

rationale: Sirach calls the community to bless the wealthy person for wonderful deeds among them. Job recalls being called blessed because he rescued the poor and helped the orphan, illustrating public praise grounded in practical help.
source_text: Who is he? We will call him happy, for he has done wonderful things among his people.

target_units.text: For an ear heard and called me blessed, and an eye that saw me turned aside.
For I rescued a poor person from a powerful man’s hand and helped an orphan who had no helper.

rationale: Sirach praises integrity when wealth offers an opportunity for wrongdoing. Job's examination of whether he trusted gold or rejoiced in amassed riches supplies a particular statement of accountability under that temptation.
source_text: Who was tested by it and brought to completion? It will be a boast for him. Who could have transgressed and did not transgress, could have done evil things and did not do them?

target_units.text: If I appointed gold as my strength, or trusted in a costly stone,
if I rejoiced because much wealth came to me, or laid my hand upon countless things,
do I not see the shining sun fail, and the moon diminish? For it does not depend on them.
And if my heart was secretly deceived, or I placed my hand upon my mouth and kissed it,
may this also be reckoned to me as the greatest lawlessness, for I lied before the Lord Most High.

rationale: Sirach links established well-being and public remembrance with almsgiving. The psalm links gifts scattered to the poor with enduring righteousness and a horn raised in glory, likewise associating generosity and lasting honor.
source_text: His good circumstances will be established, and the assembly will recount his almsgiving.

target_units.text: He scattered gifts; he gave to the poor. His righteousness remains for an age of an age; his horn will be raised in glory.

rationale: Sirach warns the guest at a great table against greedy exclamation and appetite; Proverbs tells the diner at rulers' tables to consider the food and reject insatiable desire.
source_text: Have you sat at a great table? Do not open your throat over it or say, “How much there is upon it!”

target_units.text: If you sit to dine at the table of rulers, thoughtfully consider what is set before you,
and lay your hand to it, knowing that you must prepare such things;
but if you are more insatiable, do not desire his foods, for these belong to a false life.

rationale: Sirach 31 warns against the evil eye within its meal instruction. Chapter 14 explicitly connects the evil or greedy eye with dissatisfaction over portions and begrudging bread, clarifying the concern about acquisitive looking.
source_text: Remember that an evil eye is bad. What has been created worse than an eye? Therefore it weeps for every reason.

target_units.text: Evil is the one who begrudges with his eye, turning his face away and disregarding souls.
A greedy person’s eye is not satisfied with its portion, and evil injustice dries up the soul.
An evil eye begrudges bread, and his own table is lacking.

rationale: Sirach restrains the hand that reaches greedily for a shared dish; Proverbs tells the diner to consider what is offered and not desire the food insatiably. Both require restraint in approaching a host's table.
source_text: Do not stretch your hand toward whatever it looks at, and do not crowd together with it in the dish.

target_units.text: If you sit to dine at the table of rulers, thoughtfully consider what is set before you,
and lay your hand to it, knowing that you must prepare such things;
but if you are more insatiable, do not desire his foods, for these belong to a false life.

rationale: Sirach tells the diner to understand the neighbor's concerns through his own. Jesus likewise directs treating others according to the treatment one would wish for oneself, making self-understanding a guide to consideration.
source_text: Understand your neighbor’s concerns from yourself, and consider every matter.

target_units.text: So in everything, whatever you wish people to do for you, you also do likewise for them; for this is the Law and the Prophets.

rationale: Sirach forbids greedy eating that makes a guest hated; Proverbs instructs the diner at a great table to curb insatiable desire. Both address appetite under the discipline of shared-table conduct.
source_text: Eat what is set before you like a human being, and do not chew greedily, lest you be hated.

target_units.text: If you sit to dine at the table of rulers, thoughtfully consider what is set before you,
and lay your hand to it, knowing that you must prepare such things;
but if you are more insatiable, do not desire his foods, for these belong to a false life.

rationale: Sirach says to stop eating before insatiability causes a stumble; Proverbs says to eat only sufficient honey lest fullness end in vomiting. Both counsel stopping at enough to avoid the consequence of excess.
source_text: Be the first to stop for the sake of good discipline; do not be insatiable, lest you stumble.

target_units.text: Having found honey, eat what is sufficient, lest you become full and vomit.

rationale: Sirach tells a diner among many not to reach out before the others. Paul tells those gathering to eat to wait for one another; his setting is the communal meal discussed with the Lord's supper, not an identification with Sirach's banquet.
source_text: If you have sat among many, do not stretch out your hand before them.

target_units.text: Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.

rationale: Sirach says little suffices the instructed person and avoids discomfort in bed. Proverbs likewise prescribes only sufficient honey rather than a fullness that causes vomiting, making moderation protective of the body.
source_text: How sufficient a little is for an instructed person! He does not pant upon his bed.

target_units.text: Having found honey, eat what is sufficient, lest you become full and vomit.

rationale: Sirach contrasts moderate eating and healthy sleep with excess, vomiting, and cramp. Proverbs also links excessive consumption with vomiting and counsels sufficient rather than unlimited food.
source_text: Healthy sleep comes with a moderate stomach. He rose early, and his soul was with him. The pain of sleeplessness, bilious vomiting, and cramp accompany an insatiable man.

target_units.text: Having found honey, eat what is sufficient, lest you become full and vomit.

rationale: Both ancient dietary sayings connect overeating and vomiting. Proverbs counsels moderation to prevent that result; Sirach describes a response after someone has been compelled to eat too much. The preventive and subsequent instructions remain distinct.
source_text: If you have been forced to eat too much, rise, vomit at a distance, and you will find rest.

target_units.text: Having found honey, eat what is sufficient, lest you become full and vomit.

rationale: Sirach asks the child to heed instruction and connects careful conduct with freedom from illness. Proverbs likewise asks the son to attend to its words and calls them life and healing for the flesh.
source_text: Listen to me, child, and do not despise me; in the end you will find my words true. In all your works be skillful, and no illness at all will meet you.

target_units.text: Son, attend to my utterance; apply your ear to my words,
so that your springs do not fail you; keep them in your heart,
for there is life for those who find them and healing for all flesh.

rationale: Sirach promises spoken blessing and a good reputation to the generous provider of bread; Proverbs places blessing upon the head of the person who shares grain. Both praise distribution of staple food.
source_text: Lips will bless the generous provider of bread, and testimony to his excellence is trustworthy.

target_units.text: May one who holds grain back leave it to the nations, but blessing is upon the head of one who shares it.

rationale: Sirach describes the city's complaint against stinginess with bread. Proverbs opposes withholding grain to the blessing attached to sharing it, likewise evaluating a food-holder by the treatment of others.
source_text: A city will grumble against someone stingy with bread, and testimony to his meanness is precise.
