target_units.text: May one who holds grain back leave it to the nations, but blessing is upon the head of one who shares it.

rationale: Both combine references to strength with a warning about drinking. Sirach explicitly rejects proving one's manliness through wine; Isaiah pronounces woe on strong and powerful people who drink wine and mix strong drink.
source_text: Do not show your manliness with wine, for wine has destroyed many.

target_units.text: Woe to your strong ones who drink wine and the powerful who mix strong drink,

rationale: Sirach says wine tests hearts in the proud person's quarrel; Proverbs calls drunkenness insolent and incompatible with wisdom. Both make intoxication disclose undisciplined, arrogant conduct.
source_text: A furnace tests hardened metal in quenching; so wine tests hearts in the quarrel of the proud.

target_units.text: Wine is undisciplined, and drunkenness insolent, and everyone who mingles with it will not be wise.

rationale: Sirach says wine was created for human gladness, while insisting on measure. The psalm places wine that gladdens the human heart among God's provisions; it does not separately state Sirach's measure requirement.
source_text: Wine is like life for human beings if you drink it in its measure. What is life for someone lacking wine? It too was created for human gladness.

target_units.text: and wine gladdens the human heart, to brighten the face with oil, and bread makes the human heart firm.

rationale: Sirach describes appropriately timed, measured wine as joy of heart and soul. Ecclesiastes likewise commends drinking wine with a good heart alongside glad eating, sharing the positive valuation without specifying quantity.
source_text: Wine drunk at the proper time in sufficient measure is rejoicing of heart and gladness of soul.

target_units.text: Come, eat your bread with gladness and drink your wine with a good heart, for God has already favored your deeds.

rationale: Sirach connects excessive wine with bitterness, provocation, and conflict. Proverbs describes lingering over wine as producing uproar, lawsuits, bruises, crooked speech, and disorientation, spelling out that destructive pattern.
source_text: Wine drunk in quantity amid provocation and conflict is bitterness of soul.

target_units.text: Who has woe? Who has uproar? Who has a lawsuit? Who has unpleasantness and chatter? Who has bruises for nothing? Whose eyes are livid?
Is it not those who linger over wines? Is it not those who track down where drinking parties take place?
Do not become drunk with wine, but associate with righteous people, and converse during walks; for if you give your eyes to bowls and cups, afterward you will walk about barer than a pestle.
But at the end he lies stretched out as though struck by a snake, and as though by a horned viper its poison spreads through him.
When your eyes see another woman, then your mouth will speak crooked things,
and you will lie down as in the heart of the sea, and like a helmsman in heavy surging;
and you will say, “They strike me, and I felt no pain; they mocked me, but I did not know. When will dawn come, so that I may go and seek those with whom I will gather?”

rationale: Sirach's drunken fool gains anger, stumbling, weakness, and wounds. Proverbs' drinkers acquire bruises, unstable movement, and repeated blows without awareness, showing the bodily and behavioral damage of intoxication.
source_text: Drunkenness multiplies a fool’s anger to his stumbling, diminishing strength and adding wounds.

rationale: Sirach tells the appointed leader to remain among the others and serve before sitting. Jesus likewise places the leader in the role of servant and describes Himself among those at table as the one serving.
source_text: Have they appointed you leader? Do not exalt yourself. Be among them as one of them; take care of them, and then sit down.

target_units.text: But you are not to be so. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as the one who serves.
For who is greater, the one reclining at table or the one serving? Is it not the one reclining? But I am among you as the One who serves.

rationale: Sirach's banquet leader completes duties before enjoying the meal and receiving honor. Jesus' prudent steward distributes the household's grain and is blessed when found performing that duty; both connect faithful service and favorable recognition.
source_text: After attending to every duty, recline, so that you may rejoice because of them and receive a crown for good order.

target_units.text: And the Lord said, “Who, then, is the faithful steward, the prudent one, whom his master will appoint over his household staff to give out their ration of grain at the proper time?
Blessed is that slave whom his master finds doing so when he comes.

rationale: Sirach grants the elder a fitting opportunity to speak with knowledge. Elihu explains his initial silence by his expectation that years should speak wisdom; his following words question whether age guarantees wisdom, so this parallel concerns the initial deference only.
source_text: Speak, elder, for it is fitting for you, with exact knowledge, but do not hinder the music.

target_units.text: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite replied: “I am younger in time, and you are older; therefore I kept quiet, afraid to announce my own knowledge to you.
I said, ‘Time is what speaks, and in many years people know wisdom.’

rationale: Sirach identifies a musical performance as an unsuitable time for chatter or displaying wisdom. Ecclesiastes distinguishes a time for silence from a time for speech, supplying the general timing principle applied at the banquet.
source_text: Where there is a performance, do not pour out chatter or display wisdom at an unsuitable time.

target_units.text: a time to tear and a time to sew, a time to be silent and a time to speak,

rationale: Sirach compares well-placed music at a banquet to a gem in gold. Proverbs compares a spoken wise word to precious stones in golden adornment; both use the fitting jewelry setting to praise an apt auditory contribution.
source_text: A carbuncle signet upon a golden ornament—so is an ensemble of musicians at a wine banquet.

target_units.text: A golden apple on a carnelian necklace—so is speaking a word.
A costly carnelian is fastened into a golden earring—a wise word into a receptive ear.

rationale: Sirach's melody with pleasant wine resembles an emerald in gold; Proverbs' wise word to a receptive ear resembles a costly stone set in a golden earring. Both praise an appropriate pairing through a jewel and its setting.
source_text: An emerald signet in a gold setting—so is musicians’ melody with pleasant wine.

target_units.text: A costly carnelian is fastened into a golden earring—a wise word into a receptive ear.

rationale: Sirach restrains the younger person's contribution until it is called for. Elihu describes holding back because he is young and his hearers older, showing deferential restraint before presenting his knowledge.
source_text: Speak, young man, if you are needed; scarcely twice, if you are asked.

target_units.text: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite replied: “I am younger in time, and you are older; therefore I kept quiet, afraid to announce my own knowledge to you.
I said, ‘Time is what speaks, and in many years people know wisdom.’

rationale: Sirach recommends summing up much in few words and remaining capable of silence. Ecclesiastes likewise commands few words and opposes them to a fool's many words, specifically applying its restraint before God.
source_text: Sum up your speech, much in few words; be like someone who knows and at the same time keeps silent.

target_units.text: Do not be hasty with your mouth, and do not let your heart hurry to bring out a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few.
For a dream comes with much distraction, and a fool’s voice with many words.

rationale: Sirach forbids treating oneself as a dignitary's equal or chattering over another. Proverbs forbids self-promotion into rulers' places and prefers receiving an invitation to being publicly lowered.
source_text: Among dignitaries do not make yourself their equal, and while another speaks do not chatter much.

target_units.text: Do not boast before a king, and do not station yourself in the places of rulers;
for it is better for you to be told, “Come up to me,” than for him to humble you before a ruler. Say what your eyes have seen.

rationale: Sirach says grace goes before the modest person; James says God gives grace to the humble while opposing the proud. Both attach grace to humility rather than self-exaltation.
source_text: Lightning hastens before thunder, and grace will go ahead of a modest person.

target_units.text: But He gives greater grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

rationale: Sirach advises leaving the banquet at the proper hour and returning home; Proverbs advises limiting the frequency of visits before the friend grows weary. Both set bounds on a guest’s presence, though one concerns departure and the other frequency.
source_text: Rise at the right hour and do not linger at the rear; hurry home and do not be slack.

target_units.text: Bring your foot rarely to your own friend, lest he become filled with you and hate you.

rationale: Sirach permits private enjoyment but prohibits sinning through a proud word. James expressly calls boastful pretension evil, matching the warning about arrogant speech rather than condemning enjoyment itself.
source_text: There enjoy yourself and carry out your thoughts, but do not sin by a proud word.

target_units.text: But now you boast in your pretensions. All such boasting is evil.

rationale: Sirach tells the recipient of good things to bless the Maker. Deuteronomy commands blessing the Lord after eating and being filled from the good land He gave, joining enjoyment of provision to gratitude.
source_text: For these things bless your Maker, who intoxicates you with His good things.

target_units.text: And you shall eat and be filled, and bless the Lord your God upon the good land which He has given you.

rationale: Sirach links fear of the Lord with receiving instruction. Proverbs makes reverence the beginning of perception and contrasts it with the ungodly person's rejection of wisdom and discipline.
source_text: The one who fears the Lord will receive instruction, and those who rise early will find favor.

target_units.text: The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, and good understanding belongs to all who practice it. Reverence toward God is the beginning of perception, but the ungodly will despise wisdom and discipline.

rationale: Sirach commends seeking and being filled with the law rather than stumbling hypocritically in it. The psalm describes the person whose will and continual meditation are in the Lord's law as a fruitful, flourishing tree.
source_text: The one who seeks the law will be filled with it, but the hypocrite will stumble in it.

target_units.text: Blessed is the man who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, and did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the seat of pestilent men;
but his will is in the Lord’s law, and on His law he will meditate day and night.
He will be like the tree planted beside the outlets of waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and whose leaf will not fall off; and everything he does will be prospered.

rationale: Sirach's God-fearing person kindles ordinances like light; the psalm calls God's word a lamp for the feet and a light for the path. Both portray divine instruction as illumination for conduct.
source_text: Those who fear the Lord will find judgment and kindle ordinances like light.

target_units.text: Fourteen: Noun. Thy word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.

rationale: Sirach's sinner turns rebuke aside and adapts interpretation to his own will. Proverbs contrasts the evil person's hostile response to correction with the wise person's loving and teachable response.
source_text: A sinful person will turn aside a rebuke and find an interpretation according to his own will.

target_units.text: One who disciplines evil people will receive dishonor for himself, and one who reproves an impious person will bring blame on himself.
Do not reprove evil people, so that they may not hate you; reprove a wise person, and he will love you.
Give a wise person a starting point, and he will be wiser; inform a righteous person, and he will receive still more.

rationale: Sirach's person of counsel does not disregard a considered thought. Proverbs likewise marks the wise person by listening to counsel, in contrast with the fool who regards his own way as upright.
source_text: A man of counsel will certainly not disregard a thought; an alien and proud person will not shrink from fear.

target_units.text: The ways of fools are upright before them, but a wise person listens to counsel.

rationale: Sirach requires counsel before action to prevent later regret. Proverbs criticizes dishonoring councils and says counsel remains with deliberating people, valuing consultation in forming plans.
source_text: Do nothing without counsel, and after doing it, do not regret it.

target_units.text: Those who do not honor councils put plans off, but counsel remains in the hearts of those who deliberate.

rationale: Sirach warns against an obstructed road and stumbling among stones. Proverbs instructs the learner to straighten tracks, direct ways rightly, and turn the foot from evil, using the traveled path to teach careful conduct.
source_text: Do not walk on a road of obstacles, and do not stumble among stones.

target_units.text: Make straight tracks for your feet and direct your ways rightly.
Do not turn to the right or the left; turn your foot away from an evil way.

rationale: Sirach cautions against trusting an apparently unobstructed path. Paul cautions the person who thinks he stands to take care against falling; both warn that apparent security does not remove the need for vigilance.
source_text: Do not trust a road free of stumbling blocks,

target_units.text: So let the one who thinks he stands take care that he does not fall.

rationale: Sirach extends caution even to one's children. Micah describes children dishonoring parents and enemies arising within the household, giving a concrete reason why kinship alone does not guarantee safety.
source_text: and guard yourself even against your children.

target_units.text: For a son dishonors his father, a daughter will rise against her mother, a daughter-in-law will rise against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are all the men in his house.

rationale: Sirach 32 tells the learner to trust the soul in undertaking action. Chapter 37 similarly commends the heart's counsel and the soul's watchfulness, while adding petition to the Most High for a straight path in truth.
source_text: In every undertaking trust your soul, for this too is keeping commandments.

target_units.text: Establish the counsel of your heart, for you have nothing more trustworthy than it.
For a man’s soul is sometimes accustomed to report more than seven watchmen seated high upon a watchtower.
Besides all these things, petition the Most High to make your road straight in truth.

rationale: Sirach joins trusting the law and attending to commandments with confidence in the Lord. The psalm describes lovers of God's law as having great peace and no stumbling block, likewise linking adherence to the law with stability.
source_text: The one who trusts the law attends to commandments, and the one who trusts the Lord will not be diminished.

target_units.text: Great peace belongs to those who love Thy law, and there is no stumbling block for them.

rationale: Sirach promises renewed rescue to the God-fearing person even during testing. The psalm acknowledges many afflictions of the righteous and promises the Lord's rescue from all, preserving the presence of trouble as well as deliverance.
source_text: Evil will not meet the one who fears the Lord; even in testing he will be rescued again.

target_units.text: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and He will rescue them from them all.

rationale: Sirach compares hypocritical engagement with the law to a ship in a storm. James compares divided, doubtful faith to a wind-driven sea wave and calls it unstable; both use storm-tossed water to portray inner inconsistency.
source_text: A wise man will not hate the law, but the one who acts hypocritically in it is like a ship in a storm.

target_units.text: But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.
For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord,
a man of divided mind, unstable in all his ways.

rationale: Sirach likens the law's trustworthiness to an answer from sacred tokens. Exodus places Manifestation and Truth on the oracle-piece of judgment carried by Aaron before the Lord, supplying the sacred judgment setting for that comparison.
source_text: An understanding person will trust the law, and the law is trustworthy for him, like an answer from the sacred tokens.

target_units.text: And you shall set Manifestation and Truth upon the oracle-piece of judgment; and it shall be upon Aaron’s breast when he enters into the sanctuary before the Lord. And Aaron shall bear the judgments of the sons of Israel upon his breast before the Lord continually.

rationale: Sirach requires preparing speech and gathering instruction before answering. Proverbs contrasts righteous hearts meditating on faithful things with impious mouths answering evil, similarly locating the quality of the answer in prior inward consideration.
source_text: Prepare your speech, and so you will be heard; bind instruction together and answer.

target_units.text: The hearts of the righteous meditate on faithful things, but the mouth of the impious answers evil things.

rationale: Sirach 33 describes a fool's deliberation as a rotating axle and wheel; chapter 27 contrasts godly wisdom with a fool changing like the moon. Both recurring-motion images portray the fool's instability.
source_text: A fool’s inward parts are a cartwheel, and his deliberation is like a turning axle.

target_units.text: A godly person’s discourse is always wisdom, but a fool changes like the moon.

rationale: Sirach's question about unequal days begins with their shared solar light. Genesis assigns the heavenly lights the marking of seasons, days, and years, providing the created calendar within which Sirach asks about sacred distinctions.
source_text: Why does one day surpass another when all the light of the year’s days comes from the sun?

target_units.text: And God said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to give light upon the earth and to divide the day from the night. Let them serve for signs and seasons, for days and years.

rationale: Sirach attributes differentiated seasons and festivals to the Lord's knowledge. Leviticus identifies the appointed feasts and holy convocations as the Lord's and commands their proclamation at proper times.
source_text: By the Lord’s knowledge they were distinguished, and He differentiated seasons and festivals.

target_units.text: Speak unto the sons of Israel, and you shall say unto them: The feasts of the Lord, which you shall proclaim as holy convocations, these are My feasts.
You shall do work for six days; but on the seventh day is a Sabbath, a rest, a holy convocation unto the Lord; you shall do no work; it is a Sabbath unto the Lord in every dwelling of yours.
These are the feasts for the Lord, holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at their proper times.

rationale: Sirach says God sanctified certain days while leaving others ordinary. Genesis gives the particular example of God blessing and hallowing the seventh day after His creative work.
source_text: Some He raised high and sanctified, and some He placed among the ordinary numbered days.

target_units.text: And God blessed the seventh day and hallowed it, because on it He rested from all the works that God had begun to make.

rationale: Sirach expressly says Adam was created from earth and all humans come from the ground. Genesis narrates God forming the human from earthly dust and giving him the breath of life.
source_text: All human beings are from the ground, and Adam was created from earth.

target_units.text: And God formed man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

rationale: Sirach describes the Lord's knowledgeable distinction among human beings and their ways. Moses says God knows those who are His and holy and brings those He chooses near, a particular instance of divine differentiation.
source_text: In abundant knowledge the Lord distinguished them and differentiated their ways.

target_units.text: And he said to Korah and all his congregation, God has looked upon and known those who are His and those who are holy, and has brought them near to Himself. Those He chose for Himself He brought near to Himself.

rationale: Sirach contrasts people God raises and brings near with people brought low. Hannah's song likewise says the Lord makes poor and rich, humbles and raises high, and lifts the needy to a throne of glory.
source_text: Some He blessed and raised high, some He sanctified and brought near Himself; some He cursed and brought low, and overturned them from their position.

target_units.text: The Lord makes poor and makes rich; He humbles and raises high.
He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to seat them with rulers of peoples and grant them a throne of glory as their inheritance,

rationale: Both compare the Maker's authority over people with a potter's authority over clay. Sirach emphasizes repayment according to judgment; Romans illustrates differing vessels made from the same lump for honor or dishonor.
source_text: Like a potter’s clay in his hand—all its ways are according to his pleasure—so are human beings in the hand of their Maker, for Him to repay them according to His judgment.

target_units.text: But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is formed say to the One who formed it, “Why didst Thou make me this way?”
Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

rationale: Sirach sets good against evil and life against death before contrasting sinner and godly person. Deuteronomy explicitly places the same two pairs, life and death and good and evil, before its hearers.
source_text: Good stands opposite evil, and life opposite death; so a sinner stands opposite a godly person.

target_units.text: Behold, I have set before your face this day life and death, good and evil.

rationale: Both passages describe the Most High's works as paired, one opposite another. Chapter 42 adds that nothing is deficient and that one confirms the other's good, elaborating the ordered pairing named in chapter 33.
source_text: Look in this way at all the Most High’s works: two by two, one opposite the other.

target_units.text: All things are paired, one opposite another, and He has made nothing deficient.
One has confirmed the good things of another. Who will be filled with beholding His glory?

rationale: Within Sirach 33:16-18 the late gleaner image describes gathering instruction for others. Ecclesiastes likewise describes a wise teacher teaching the people knowledge and seeking truthful written words; the agricultural image belongs only to Sirach.
source_text: I too, the last, kept watch like someone gleaning behind grape-gatherers.

target_units.text: Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.
Ecclesiastes sought much to find words of delight and something written in uprightness, words of truth.

rationale: Sirach's filled winepress continues its image of successfully gathered instruction, as clarified by 33:18. Ecclesiastes describes collected wise words, their ordered arrangement, and their gift from one shepherd; the comparison concerns the gathered teaching, not a literal harvest.
source_text: By the Lord’s blessing I came in time, and like a grape-gatherer I filled a winepress.

target_units.text: Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.
Ecclesiastes sought much to find words of delight and something written in uprightness, words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads and like planted nails, which were given from collections, from one shepherd, and something beyond them.

rationale: Sirach says his labor serves everyone seeking instruction rather than himself alone. Ecclesiastes likewise describes the wise author teaching the people knowledge.
source_text: Consider that I have labored not for myself alone, but for all who seek instruction.

target_units.text: Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.

rationale: Both summon public leaders to listen and learn. Sirach addresses dignitaries and assembly leaders; Wisdom addresses kings, judges, and rulers of multitudes with the same call to give ear.
source_text: Listen to me, dignitaries of the people; give ear, leaders of the assembly.

target_units.text: Listen, then, kings, and understand; learn, judges of the ends of the earth.
Give ear, you who rule a multitude and boast over crowds of nations;

rationale: Sirach warns the living person not to exchange himself for any human being. Paul tells those bought at a price not to become slaves of humans; the resistance to human subjection is shared, with Paul's distinct theological reason retained.
source_text: As long as you still live and breath is in you, do not exchange yourself for any flesh.

target_units.text: You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings.

rationale: Sirach prefers children depending on the parent to the parent depending on the children's hands. Paul likewise says parents should store up for children rather than children for parents, using that family expectation to explain his own conduct.
source_text: For it is better that your children ask you than that you look toward your sons’ hands.

target_units.text: Look, for the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not be a burden. For I seek not what is yours but you; for the children ought not to store up for the parents, but the parents for the children.

rationale: Sirach locates inheritance distribution at the completion of life. Hebrews explains that a testament takes effect at the maker's death and is not in force during his life, connecting inheritance arrangements to that same transition.
source_text: On the day when your life’s days are completed, at the time of death, distribute your inheritance.

target_units.text: For where there is a testament, the death of the one who made it must be established.
For a testament takes effect at death, since it is never in force while the one who made it lives.

rationale: Sirach places the donkey's rod and burdens beside the household slave's discipline and work. Proverbs compares horse and donkey restraints with a rod for a lawless nation; both ancient disciplinary analogies transfer animal-control imagery to human settings without naming the same human group.
source_text: Fodder, a rod, and burdens for a donkey; bread, discipline, and work for a household slave.

target_units.text: As a whip for a horse and a goad for a donkey, so a rod for a lawless nation.

rationale: Sirach prescribes coercive restraints and torture for a wrongdoing household slave. Exodus addresses a master's beating of an enslaved person with a rod and distinguishes liability by the outcome. The comparison records ancient treatment and legal limits rather than equating their prescriptions.
source_text: A yoke and strap will bend a neck, and racks and tortures are for a wrongdoing household slave.

target_units.text: And if a man strikes his male slave or his female slave with a rod, and the slave dies under his hands, he shall surely be avenged by judgment.
But if the slave survives a day or two, he shall not be avenged; for he is his silver.

rationale: Sirach associates idleness with learning evil and therefore assigns work to the servant. Paul describes certain widows learning idleness and becoming gossips and busybodies; both link inactivity with learned misconduct, while addressing different groups.
source_text: Put him to work so that he is not idle, for idleness has taught much evil.

target_units.text: And at the same time they learn to be idle, going around the houses, and not only idle but also gossips and busybodies, saying things they ought not to say.

rationale: Sirach tells the master to assign tasks and increase fetters for disobedience. Ephesians addresses masters with a contrasting restraint: give up threats, remembering the impartial heavenly Master. Their distinct approaches to coercion are preserved.
source_text: Assign him tasks as befits him, and if he does not obey, make his fetters heavy.

target_units.text: And masters, act in the same way toward them, giving up threats, knowing that both their Master and yours is in the heavens, and there is no partiality with Him.

rationale: Within household discipline Sirach prohibits excess against any person and requires judgment. Colossians likewise requires masters to provide what is just and equitable to enslaved people, grounding that duty in their own accountability to a heavenly Master.
source_text: Do not go to excess against any flesh, and do nothing without judgment.

target_units.text: Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and equitable, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.

rationale: Sirach tells the owner to regard the household slave as himself. Paul asks that Onesimus be received as a beloved brother and welcomed as Paul himself; both require personal or familial regard for the enslaved person, while giving distinct reasons.
source_text: If you have a household slave, let him be as yourself, because you acquired him with blood.

target_units.text: no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
So if you regard me as a partner, welcome him as you would me.

rationale: Sirach explicitly requires treating the household slave as a brother. Paul likewise asks that Onesimus be received as more than a slave, a beloved brother in the flesh and in the Lord, extending the familial description in a Christian setting.
source_text: If you have a household slave, treat him as a brother, because you will need him as your own soul.

target_units.text: no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

rationale: Sirach warns that mistreatment can make an enslaved person flee beyond recovery. Deuteronomy addresses the person who escapes a master and forbids returning or oppressing him, viewing the same flight from the receiving community's protective obligation.
source_text: If you mistreat him and he leaves and runs away, on what road will you look for him?

target_units.text: You shall not deliver unto his master a slave who has come unto you from his master.
He shall dwell with you; he shall dwell among you in any place that pleases him. You shall not afflict him.
